slides.title: Welcome to Fermentation Technology
slides.content:
# Fermentation Technology

Welcome to **Fermentation Technology**!

## What You Will Learn:
- **Bioreactor design** - The heart of the process
- **Scale-up parameters** - Moving from the lab to the factory
- **Aeration and agitation** - Keeping cells breathing
- **Sterilization** - Keeping the bad bugs out

Fermentation is the process of using living cells to mass-produce valuable products, from beer to life-saving antibodies.

slides.title: What is a Bioreactor?
slides.content:
# The Bioreactor

A bioreactor (or fermenter) is a highly controlled, engineered vessel designed to provide the perfect environment for cells to grow and produce.

## The Goal:
The goal is to carefully control temperature, pH, dissolved oxygen, and nutrient levels to keep millions (or billions) of cells as happy and productive as possible.

slides.title: Types of Bioreactors
slides.content:
# Bioreactor Design

## 1. Stirred-Tank Reactor (STR):
The industry standard. It looks like a giant metal soup pot with a mechanical propeller (impeller) in the center to mix everything vigorously.

## 2. Airlift Reactor:
Instead of a mechanical propeller, air is pumped into the bottom of the tank. As the bubbles rise, they drag the liquid up with them, creating a gentle, natural circulation. Great for fragile cells!

slides.title: Materials and Sensors
slides.content:
# Engineering the Vessel

Bioreactors must be built from highly polished stainless steel. Any microscopic scratch could hide unwanted bacteria.

## The Sensory Array:
A modern bioreactor bristles with sensors:
- **pH probes** (to add acid/base as needed)
- **Dissolved Oxygen (DO) probes**
- **Temperature sensors** (wrapped in cooling jackets because billions of cells generate massive amounts of body heat!)

slides.title: Scale-Up Parameters
slides.content:
# The Scale-Up Challenge

Growing cells in a 1-liter glass flask in a lab is easy. Growing them in a 20,000-liter steel tank is incredibly difficult.

## The Problem of Volume:
As you scale up, the volume of liquid increases much faster than the surface area of the tank. 

This means it becomes mathematically much harder to mix the liquid evenly, push oxygen into the center of the tank, and remove the heat generated by the cells.

slides.title: Bioreactor Quiz
slides.content: Test your knowledge of bioreactor design.
slides.quizQuestion: Why might a bioprocess engineer choose an Airlift Reactor instead of a standard Stirred-Tank Reactor?
quizOptions: Because Airlift reactors are cheaper to build
Because the cells being grown are physically fragile and would be shredded by a mechanical propeller
Because Airlift reactors can only be used to grow plant cells
Because mechanical propellers consume too much electricity

slides.title: Rules of Thumb for Scale-Up
slides.content:
# Scale-Up Strategies

Engineers use mathematical rules to keep conditions the same as they build bigger tanks.

1. **Geometric Similarity:** The large tank must have the exact same height-to-width proportions as the small lab flask.
2. **Constant Power Input:** They calculate the mechanical power of the mixer per unit volume, ensuring the large tank mixes with the same relative violence as the small one.
3. **Tip Speed:** Ensuring the edge of the propeller doesn't move so fast that it breaks the cells.

slides.title: Aeration and Mass Transfer
slides.content:
# Keeping Cells Breathing

Cells need oxygen to grow. But oxygen gas does not dissolve easily into water (liquid broth).

## Mass Transfer:
The hardest job of a bioreactor is forcing oxygen molecules to jump from an air bubble into the liquid, a process called Mass Transfer.

If the cells at the bottom of the tank use up all the oxygen before new oxygen dissolves, the batch will die (suffocation).

slides.title: Agitation and Sparging
slides.content:
# Agitation Strategies

To maximize oxygen mass transfer, you must maximize the surface area of the air bubbles.

## The Sparger and the Impeller:
Air is blasted into the bottom of the tank through a ring with tiny holes (the Sparger).

Immediately above the sparger is the Impeller (propeller). The impeller violently smashes the large air bubbles into millions of microscopic bubbles, drastically increasing the surface area for oxygen to dissolve into the liquid!

slides.title: Shear Stress
slides.content:
# The Danger of Shear Stress

There is a fine line between mixing well and murdering your cells.

## Shear Stress:
If you spin the impeller too fast to break up the bubbles, the mechanical friction of the rushing water (Shear Stress) will physically rip the cell membranes apart.

Engineers must perfectly balance the need for high oxygen (fast mixing) against the fragility of the cells (slow mixing).

slides.title: Sterilization
slides.content:
# The Threat of Contamination

Your bioreactor is a paradise: perfect temperature, endless sugar, zero predators. 

If even ONE single wild bacterial cell from the air gets into your 20,000-liter tank, it will multiply, steal all the food, and ruin millions of dollars worth of product.

The entire system must be absolutely sterile before you begin.

slides.title: Aeration Quiz
slides.content: Verify your understanding of mass transfer.
slides.quizQuestion: Why does a bioreactor impeller intentionally smash large air bubbles into microscopic bubbles?
quizOptions: To make the liquid look prettier
To drastically increase the surface area of the air, allowing oxygen to dissolve into the liquid much faster
To prevent the bubbles from floating to the top

slides.title: Thermal Death Kinetics
slides.content:
# Heat Sterilization

The most reliable way to kill everything is heat (usually high-pressure steam at 121 degrees Celsius).

## Thermal Death Kinetics:
Killing bacteria is a logarithmic process. If 1 minute of steam kills 90% of bacteria, 2 minutes kills 99%, 3 minutes kills 99.9%, and so on.

Engineers calculate exactly how many minutes of steam are required to reduce the probability of a single surviving cell to less than 1 in a million.

slides.title: Batch vs Continuous Sterilization
slides.content:
# Sterilizing the Broth

## Batch Sterilization:
You fill the tank with the liquid food (media), heat the entire tank to 121 degrees, hold it, and cool it. Very slow, and the long cooking time often destroys sensitive vitamins in the food.

## Continuous Sterilization:
You pump the liquid through a tiny, incredibly hot pipe for just a few seconds, then instantly cool it as it enters the sterile tank. Faster, and preserves the vitamins!

slides.title: Filter Sterilization
slides.content:
# Sterilizing the Air

Cells need millions of liters of air pumped into the tank over the course of a week. You cannot heat-sterilize air fast enough.

## Depth and Membrane Filters:
All air entering (and leaving) the tank must pass through highly specialized filters with pores as small as 0.2 micrometers.

These pores are physically smaller than the smallest known bacteria, guaranteeing that the air entering the tank is 100% sterile.

slides.title: Summary of Fermentation Technology
slides.content:
# Fermentation Summary

## Key Takeaways:
- **Bioreactors** (Stirred-Tank or Airlift) provide a perfectly controlled environment for mass cell culture.
- **Scale-Up** is a massive mathematical challenge due to changing volume-to-surface-area ratios.
- **Aeration** relies on the impeller smashing bubbles to maximize oxygen mass transfer without causing fatal **Shear Stress**.
- Absolute **Sterilization** using steam kinetics and micro-filtration is required to prevent catastrophic contamination.
